What local content actually means in Namibia

By the Katelago HR team

Local content is the phrase everyone in Namibian oil and gas is using at the moment, and it is being used to mean at least four different things. Before a business can plan around it, someone has to say plainly what it is, what already binds you, and what does not.

That is what this guide does.

The definition

The draft upstream petroleum local content policy defines local content as the added value to the Namibian economy through the use of Namibian labour, goods and services, companies, ownership and financing in the upstream petroleum sector.

So it is broader than jobs. It covers five things: who you employ, what you buy, who you buy it from, who owns those suppliers, and where the money is raised.

Upstream only

The policy is an upstream policy. Upstream means finding and producing oil and gas: exploration, appraisal, development and production. Refining, distribution and fuel retail are downstream and sit outside it. We explain the words in the oil and gas terms guide.

Three layers, and only two of them bind anyone today

This is the part that gets confused most often, so it is worth setting out carefully.

Layer one: section 14 of the Petroleum Act. Binding since 1992.

The Petroleum (Exploration and Production) Act 2 of 1991 already contains local content obligations, and it has done for over thirty years. Section 14 makes it a condition of every licence that the holder must:

  1. give preference to Namibian citizens with appropriate qualifications when employing people
  2. carry out training programmes to encourage and promote the development of those citizens in its employment
  3. make use of products, equipment and services available in Namibia, after due regard to technical and economic efficiency
  4. co-operate with others in the industry so that Namibians can develop the skills and technology to serve the industry

The Act also allows the Minister to enter into agreements with licence holders on training programmes and on contributions to the Petroleum Training and Education Fund.

Two things to notice. First, these are conditions of the licence, so breach is a licence compliance matter rather than an ordinary contractual dispute. Second, and this is the crucial point, section 14 contains no numbers at all. It is qualitative. There is no statutory percentage of Namibian employees, no procurement quota and no ownership threshold anywhere in the Act.

Layer two: the petroleum agreement. Binding on the parties to it.

Alongside the Act sits the Model Petroleum Agreement, and each operator signs its own agreement with the State. Those agreements carry clauses on employment and training, on the use of Namibian goods and services, and on domestic supply.

If there are numbers anywhere, this is where they live. And here is the practical difficulty for anyone tendering into the sector: Namibian petroleum agreements are not published. So when a contractor asks what percentage of Namibians an operator has committed to, the honest answer is that only the operator and the State know, and the answer differs from block to block.

Layer three: the local content policy. Approved, but not yet law.

Cabinet approved the National Upstream Petroleum Local Content Policy on 4 August 2026, after regional consultations through 2025 and an approval in principle in April 2026.

That is a genuine milestone. But a policy is not a law. This one has not been gazetted, which is the step that would give it legal force, and the approved text has not been publicly released. As things stand, no operator carries a binding obligation under it, and no percentage targets have been published.

Government has said that legislation will follow. The labour ministry confirmed in August 2026 that an appropriate legislative framework is needed. No bill has been introduced.

What this means if someone tells you the policy requires something

Ask which layer they are talking about. If it is section 14, they are right and it has always been true. If it is a specific operator's agreement, they may be right but neither of you can check it. If it is the policy, it is direction of travel rather than obligation, at least for now.

What the policy is likely to require, based on the published draft

The approved text is not public, but the 2023 draft is, and the shape is unlikely to have changed fundamentally. Read this as an indication of where things are going, not as a current requirement.

Themes in the published draft policy
AreaWhat the draft proposes
EmploymentPreference for suitably qualified Namibians, Namibians to fill all unskilled positions, and a progressive increase in Namibian representation in professional, technical and managerial roles, phased after significant discoveries
TrainingMeaningful training and development treated as a requirement of operating in the sector, delivered through mentorships, understudies, succession plans and secondments
ProcurementPreference for Namibian suppliers on competitive standards, contracts unbundled so local firms can actually bid, local advertising, and tender evaluation that weights local value added
OwnershipA local company defined as at least 51 percent owned by Namibian citizens with its principal place of business in Namibia, plus measures against fronting
ReportingA local content plan at petroleum agreement stage and again at field development plan stage, with annual reporting against commitments
TargetsSoft targets initially, given how young the sector is, with prescriptive targets introduced on a graduated basis after consultation with industry

The employment and training language in that draft mirrors something that already binds many Namibian employers, which we come back to below.

The only official numbers published so far

The Sixth National Development Plan sets government planning targets for the sector over 2025/26 to 2029/30. These are national goals rather than obligations on any employer, but they are published and they tell you what government is aiming at.

NDP6 oil and gas indicators
IndicatorBaseline 2024Target 2030
Jobs created in the sector2,80022,800
Local content and carried participation, percent1015
Oil production, million barrels of oil equivalent0150

A jump from roughly 2,800 to 22,800 jobs in six years is the number worth sitting with. If it is anywhere near right, the constraint will not be demand for Namibian workers. It will be the supply of Namibians with the qualifications and the documented experience to be appointed.

The obligation that already binds you, today

While the sector waits for local content legislation, there is a Namibian law that already requires skills transfer and it is widely ignored.

Section 19(3) of the Affirmative Action (Employment) Act 29 of 1998 requires a relevant employer to train a Namibian citizen as the understudy of every non-Namibian citizen it employs. The Minister may exempt where the trade or profession is too specialised or where training is impractical.

That is far more concrete than anything in the local content policy. It is enforced through the affirmative action reporting cycle and the compliance certificate, and without a valid certificate you cannot be given a State contract, guarantee, loan, licence, permit, grant or concession.

For a business hoping to serve the oil and gas sector, that last sentence is the whole argument. We cover it in the Affirmative Action reporting guide and in employing non-Namibians in the sector.

An honest word about the debate

Local content is not universally welcomed, and it is worth knowing the criticisms rather than being surprised by them. Economists have warned that requirements of this kind can create middleman arrangements that raise costs without building capability. Industry voices have argued the opposite way, that the policy lacks enforcement teeth because it carries no penalties.

Both can be true. A local content regime works when it builds real Namibian capability and fails when it simply inserts a Namibian name between an international contractor and a contract. The difference is usually visible in one place: whether the local partner actually employs and trains people.

Which is, in the end, an HR question rather than a policy one. Businesses that can show a real workforce, real training records and real compliance documents will do well out of this. Those that cannot will find that the paperwork catches up with them.

What to do now

  1. Get your Affirmative Action position in order, including the understudy requirement and a valid compliance certificate.
  2. Document your workforce properly: who is Namibian, who is not, what qualifications and training each person holds.
  3. Build genuine training and understudy programmes rather than paper ones, and keep the records.
  4. Make sure your ownership and registration documents are clean and current, since a 51 percent Namibian ownership test is likely to feature.
  5. Watch for the gazetting of the policy and for the local content bill. That is when obligations become real.
